analogy.p: When the house gets warm enough, the thermostat tells the boiler to switch off (high thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH). When the house cools, the boiler comes back on (low thyroxine, so TRH and TSH are released). The house temperature is the thyroxine level and the radiators are the body cells. Adrenaline is more like a fire alarm that suddenly sets everything in motion. The analogy breaks down because a thermostat is a single device, whereas the body uses a chain of glands and hormones, and adrenaline is not about holding a level steady.
analogy.t: A central heating system with a thermostat

bullets: **Thyroxine**: made by the thyroid gland, raises the basal metabolic rate, needed for growth and development.
**Negative feedback**: a change in a level triggers a response that reverses the change and brings the level back to normal.
**Adrenaline**: made by the adrenal glands, released in fear or stress, increases heart rate and so delivers more oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.
Thyroxine control needs the **hypothalamus, pituitary gland, TRH and TSH**; learn the order.
Adrenaline is a fast emergency hormone; thyroxine is a steady, long-term background hormone.
Both are **hormones**: chemical messengers made in endocrine glands, carried in the blood plasma and acting on target organs.
Command words you will meet: **describe**, **explain**, **suggest** and **compare**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point sits inside the hormonal coordination topic in Homeostasis and response. It is a **biology-only (triple)** point. You must know that **thyroxine** is made by the **thyroid gland** and **stimulates the basal metabolic rate**, that it is important for **growth and development**, and that its level is controlled by **negative feedback**. You must also know that **adrenaline** is made by the **adrenal glands** in times of fear or stress and prepares the body for **flight or fight**. Examiners like to combine this with the general idea of homeostasis, so you should be able to explain the whole loop in the correct order.

bullets: Hormones are secreted into the blood by **endocrine glands** (there are no ducts).
They travel in the **blood plasma** to every part of the body, but only target organs respond.
Nervous responses: fast, short-lived, travel as electrical impulses. Hormonal responses: slower, longer-lasting, travel in the blood.
The **pituitary gland** is the 'master gland' because its hormones (such as TSH) control other glands.
The **hypothalamus** in the brain monitors conditions and controls the pituitary gland.
Glands in this topic: pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, ovary and testes.
Thyroid gland sits in the neck; adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys.
core.h: Hormones and the endocrine system: the background
core.p: The **endocrine system** is made of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. A **hormone** is a chemical messenger. It travels all over the body in the blood but only affects its **target organs**, which have the right receptors. Because the blood is a slower transport system than nerves, hormonal effects are usually slower to start and last longer than nervous effects. Both thyroxine and adrenaline fit this pattern, although adrenaline is quicker than most hormones because it is released during an emergency.

bullets: Step 1: the level of a variable moves away from the set point (the stimulus).
Step 2: a **receptor** detects the change.
Step 3: a **coordination centre** (brain, pancreas, pituitary and so on) receives the information and decides what to do.
Step 4: an **effector** (a muscle or gland) carries out the response.
Step 5: the response **opposes** the change, so the level moves back toward the set point.
Step 6: when it is back to normal the response switches off, so it does not overshoot.
Examples: blood glucose, body temperature, water balance, thyroxine level.
Opposite idea: **positive feedback** makes a change bigger (not needed in your GCSE spec).
core.p: Many body systems keep a variable close to its **set point**, which is a process called **homeostasis**. Negative feedback is the mechanism. When the level of something changes away from normal, receptors detect the change, a coordination centre processes the information, and effectors produce a response that **reverses the change**. Once the level is back to normal the response is reduced or switched off. It is called 'negative' because the response is in the opposite direction to the change, not because it is bad. This is why a level swings gently around the normal value rather than running out of control.

bullets: Made by: the **thyroid gland** (in the neck).
Transported by: the **blood**.
Target cells: nearly all body cells.
Effect 1: **stimulates the basal metabolic rate**, so cells release more energy by respiration.
Effect 2: important for **growth and development**, including the brain in young children.
Needs **iodine** from the diet to be made (extra context).
Level is kept steady by **negative feedback**.
core.p: The **thyroid gland** is in the neck and releases the hormone **thyroxine** into the blood. Thyroxine travels to almost every cell in the body. Its main job is to **stimulate the basal metabolic rate (BMR)**, which is the rate at which the body uses energy when it is at rest to keep vital processes such as breathing, circulation and cell chemistry going. It is also important for **growth and development**, especially in children. The body makes thyroxine using the element iodine, so a healthy diet needs enough iodine.

bullets: **Hypothalamus** detects the thyroxine level and releases **TRH**.
**TRH** acts on the pituitary gland.
**Pituitary gland** releases **TSH** into the blood.
**TSH** acts on the thyroid gland, its target organ.
**Thyroid gland** releases **thyroxine** into the blood.
Thyroxine acts on body cells and raises the BMR.
Remember: TSH is not made by the thyroid; the thyroid is the target organ for TSH.
core.h: The control chain: hypothalamus, pituitary and thyroid
core.p: The thyroid does not decide for itself how much thyroxine to make. It is controlled by a chain of signals. The **hypothalamus** in the brain monitors the level of thyroxine in the blood. When it is low, the hypothalamus releases **thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)**. TRH travels a short distance to the **pituitary gland**, which releases **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** into the blood. TSH travels to the thyroid gland (its target organ) and stimulates it to release thyroxine. Learn the order: hypothalamus, TRH, pituitary, TSH, thyroid, thyroxine.

bullets: **If thyroxine is too high**: inhibits TRH and TSH, so thyroid releases less, so the level falls.
**If thyroxine is too low**: less inhibition, so TRH and TSH rise, so the thyroid releases more, so the level rises.
The thyroxine itself is the signal that closes the loop; this is the 'feedback'.
Receptor/coordination role: the hypothalamus and pituitary monitor and respond to the level.
Effector: the **thyroid gland**.
The result is a fairly constant BMR and steady growth.
Key mark-scheme word: **inhibits**; never say 'stops completely'.
core.h: Negative feedback on thyroxine, step by step
core.p: The loop closes because thyroxine itself acts back on the hypothalamus and pituitary. When the level of thyroxine in the blood rises above normal, the high level **inhibits** the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the pituitary gland. With less TSH, the thyroid is stimulated less, so less thyroxine is released and the level falls back to normal. If the level falls too low, the inhibition is removed, TRH and TSH are released again and the thyroid makes more thyroxine. The level therefore oscillates slightly around the set point and is never allowed to run away.

bullets: The dashed horizontal line is the **set point** or normal level.
A peak above the line means thyroxine is too high, so TRH/TSH fall.
A trough below the line means thyroxine is too low, so TRH/TSH rise.
Swings usually get smaller as control takes effect.
Use data from the graph: quote values with units when asked.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100.
If TSH and thyroxine are plotted together, they move in **opposite** directions.
core.p: In exam questions the negative feedback loop is often drawn as a graph of hormone level against time. The line wobbles around a horizontal set point. After a rise above the set point the line falls, and after a fall below the set point the line rises. This shows that the response is always in the opposite direction to the change. To score full marks you must link each part of the graph to the right step in the loop, for example 'the level of thyroxine is above normal at A, so TSH release is inhibited and the level falls'.

bullets: Underactive thyroid: low thyroxine, low BMR, so feeling tired, cold, weight gain.
Overactive thyroid: high thyroxine, high BMR, so weight loss, heat, fast heart rate.
Thyroxine tablets treat an underactive thyroid.
Extra thyroxine in blood makes the pituitary release **less TSH** (negative feedback).
A lack of iodine in the diet can enlarge the thyroid (goitre); the low thyroxine means more TSH is released, which swells the gland (extra context).
This extension is not required in detail; focus on the loop.
core.p: If the thyroid makes too little thyroxine (an **underactive thyroid**, hypothyroidism) the BMR falls. People may feel tired and cold and put on weight. If it makes too much (**overactive thyroid**, hyperthyroidism) the BMR is too high and a person may lose weight, feel hot and have a fast heart rate. These are medical examples beyond what the spec requires, but they show why tight control matters. In hypothyroidism, tablets of thyroxine can replace the missing hormone. When someone takes extra thyroxine, the negative feedback loop reduces their own TSH.

bullets: Made in the **adrenal glands**, on top of the kidneys.
Triggered by **fear, stress, danger or excitement**.
Brain detects the stimulus, nerves signal the adrenal glands.
Released into the **bloodstream** and carried to target organs.
Target organs include the heart, liver, lungs and muscles.
Adrenaline works quickly and for a short time.
'Fight or flight' means either confront the danger or run from it.
core.p: **Adrenaline** is a hormone produced by the **adrenal glands**, which sit on top of the kidneys. It is released in times of **fear or stress** when the body senses danger or excitement. The brain detects the threat and sends nerve impulses to the adrenal glands, which then release adrenaline into the blood. Because the signal starts as a nervous impulse and the hormone is then carried quickly in the blood, adrenaline works much faster than most other hormones. Its job is to prepare the body for **flight or fight**.

bullets: **Heart rate rises**: blood circulates faster.
More **oxygen and glucose** are delivered to brain and muscles.
So muscles can respire faster and release more energy for movement.
Liver converts stored glycogen into glucose and releases it (increases blood glucose).
Breathing rate increases to take in more oxygen (extra detail).
Pupils widen to let in more light (extra detail).
Blood is diverted away from the digestive system toward muscles (extra detail).
Effects fade once the threat has passed.
core.h: Effects of adrenaline and why they help
core.p: The central effect to learn is that adrenaline **increases the heart rate**. A faster heart rate pumps blood around the body more quickly, which **boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles**. The muscles then have more of the raw materials for aerobic respiration, so they can release more energy for fighting or running, and the brain is alert and thinking fast. Adrenaline also makes the liver release stored glucose into the blood, widens the pupils, and increases breathing rate, so the body is fully prepared. You should always link the effect to the benefit.

bullets: Thyroxine: keeps BMR steady using negative feedback.
Adrenaline: gives a short burst response to fear or stress.
Adrenaline release is triggered by **nerve impulses** from the brain.
When the threat ends, nerve signals stop and less adrenaline is released.
The heart rate returns toward normal as adrenaline falls.
Do not call adrenaline a homeostasis hormone like insulin or thyroxine.
core.p: Thyroxine is a clear example of negative feedback that keeps a level steady. Adrenaline is different. It is released as an emergency response to a stimulus, not to hold a variable at a constant set point. Its release is controlled by the nervous system, and it stops being released when the danger or stress passes and the nervous signals stop. The hormone is then removed from the blood and its effects fade. So you should not write that adrenaline controls a set level by feedback; say it is a response to a stimulus and ends when the stimulus ends.

bullets: **Gland**: thyroid (thyroxine) versus adrenal (adrenaline).
**Trigger**: TSH from the pituitary versus nerve signals during fear or stress.
**Time scale**: thyroxine slower and longer-lasting versus adrenaline fast and short-lived.
**Effect**: raises BMR and supports growth versus raises heart rate and prepares for fight or flight.
**Control**: negative feedback versus switched off when the stimulus stops.
Both are hormones, carried in the blood, and act on target organs.
core.p: Comparison questions are common. Make sure you state a point about both hormones in every sentence and use words like 'whereas' or 'but'. The two hormones are made in different glands, released for different reasons and have different effects and time scales. Only thyroxine is described here as being controlled by negative feedback to keep a steady level.

bullets: Blood glucose: high glucose, insulin released, glucose falls; low glucose, glucagon released, glucose rises.
Temperature: skin and hypothalamus monitor, sweating or shivering restores 37 degrees C.
Water balance: ADH from the pituitary changes how much water the kidneys reabsorb.
Menstrual cycle: oestrogen inhibits FSH; progesterone maintains the uterus lining.
Respiration: adrenaline helps supply glucose and oxygen for aerobic respiration in muscles.
Circulation: adrenaline raises heart rate, linking to the heart and blood vessels topic.
Variation of hormone levels is shown in data questions on all of these.
core.p: Negative feedback is one of the most reusable ideas in GCSE Biology. The same logic of receptor, coordination centre, effector and a response that opposes the change is used in the control of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon, in the control of body temperature, and in the control of water content by ADH. In the menstrual cycle, a rising level of oestrogen inhibits FSH release, which is another negative feedback loop. Learning the general pattern lets you tackle unfamiliar hormone questions.

exam: **Describe/state (1-2 marks)**: give the facts only, e.g. 'thyroxine is made by the thyroid gland and increases the basal metabolic rate'.
**Explain (2-4 marks)**: each mark is a linked step: because...so... Use the word 'inhibits' for negative feedback.
For the thyroxine loop, aim for the sequence: hypothalamus releases TRH, pituitary releases TSH, thyroid releases thyroxine, high thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH.
**6-mark questions** need a logical, ordered answer that covers both the high and low case.
For adrenaline, always link effect to benefit: heart rate rises, so more oxygen and glucose reach muscles for respiration.
Use correct names: **hypothalamus, pituitary gland, thyroid gland, adrenal glands**.
**Compare** needs both hormones in each sentence, using 'whereas' or 'but'.
Graph questions: describe the pattern, quote values with units, then explain it using negative feedback.
Percentage change = change / original x 100; always include the % sign.
Typical mark allocations: define negative feedback (2), name the gland (1), effect of adrenaline (2-3), explain control (4).
Do not repeat the question; use the data given in the stem.

mistakes.r: Thyroxine is made by the **thyroid gland**; the pituitary makes TSH.
mistakes.w: Thyroxine is made by the pituitary gland.

mistakes.r: High thyroxine **inhibits** (reduces) the release of TRH and TSH.
Negative feedback is when a response **reverses** a change to return the level to normal.
mistakes.w: Negative feedback is when something bad happens.

mistakes.r: Thyroxine increases the **basal metabolic rate**; adrenaline raises the heart rate.
Adrenaline increases heart rate, so more **oxygen and glucose** are delivered to muscles for respiration; it does not itself give energy.
Adrenaline is released in response to fear or stress and stops when the stimulus ends.
mistakes.w: Adrenaline is controlled by negative feedback like thyroxine.

mistakes.r: TSH is made by the **pituitary**; its target organ is the thyroid.
mistakes.w: TSH is made by the thyroid.

mistakes.r: Hormones travel in the **blood**; nerves carry electrical impulses.

summary: You need to know how thyroxine from the thyroid gland stimulates the basal metabolic rate and how its level is controlled by negative feedback involving the hypothalamus, TRH, the pituitary and TSH, and how adrenaline from the adrenal glands prepares the body for flight or fight. It matters because it is a standard biology-only application of homeostasis and negative feedback.

terms.d: A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood to act on a target organ.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
The organ or tissue that has receptors for a particular hormone and so responds to it.
The gland in the neck that secretes thyroxine.
A hormone from the thyroid gland that stimulates the basal metabolic rate and is important for growth and development.
The rate at which the body uses energy at rest to keep vital processes going.
The part of the brain that monitors conditions and releases TRH, which controls the pituitary gland.
The gland at the base of the brain that releases TSH and other hormones.
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone, released by the hypothalamus to make the pituitary release TSH.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, released by the pituitary to make the thyroid release thyroxine.
A control mechanism in which a change in a level triggers a response that reverses the change and returns the level to normal.
The normal level at which a variable is kept.
The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function.
Glands on top of the kidneys that secrete adrenaline.
A hormone released in fear or stress that increases heart rate and prepares the body for flight or fight.
The body's response to danger, preparing it either to run away or to confront the threat.
To reduce or stop the release or action of something.

worked.ans: High thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH release, so the thyroid is stimulated less and releases less thyroxine; the level falls back to normal. This is negative feedback.
worked.q: Thyroxine level in a person's blood rises above normal. Explain how the level returns to normal. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: the high level of thyroxine is detected by the hypothalamus and pituitary gland.
Mark 2: high thyroxine inhibits the release of TRH from the hypothalamus.
Mark 3: and inhibits the release of TSH from the pituitary gland.
Mark 4: so the thyroid gland is stimulated less and releases less thyroxine, so the level falls back to normal.

worked.ans: Adrenaline released by the adrenal glands increases the heart rate, which boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles and brain, so more energy is released by respiration for fight or flight.
worked.q: A person is suddenly frightened. Describe and explain the effects of adrenaline on the body. (6 marks)
steps: The brain detects the fear and nerve impulses signal the adrenal glands.
The adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood.
Adrenaline travels in the blood to the heart (target organ).
The heart rate increases, so blood is pumped faster.
This boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.
So muscles can respire faster and release more energy for fight or flight.

worked.ans: 75% decrease; extra thyroxine inhibits TSH release by negative feedback.
worked.q: A patient takes thyroxine tablets. Their TSH level falls from 4.0 mU/L to 1.0 mU/L. Calculate the percentage decrease and explain the change. (3 marks)
steps: Explanation: the extra thyroxine in the blood inhibits the pituitary gland, so less TSH is released (negative feedback).
